## 1. Overview & Core Concepts

In ServiceNow, the Service Catalog acts as the digital storefront for end users to request services, equipment, access, or automated actions.

When a user submits a catalog item, ServiceNow processes the request using a 3-tier hierarchy. Understanding this structure is essential for designing forms, routing approvals, and assigning work tasks.

### 2. The 3-Tier Request Hierarchy

Every submission in the Service Catalog follows a parent-child structure:

[ Request (REQ) ]

│

└───> [ Requested Item (RITM) ]

│

├───> [ Catalog Task (SCTASK 1) ]

└───> [ Catalog Task (SCTASK 2) ]

### Breakdown of Hierarchy Levels

Request (REQ): The top-level shopping cart container. It tracks overall order details, overall cost, and who placed the order. A single REQ can contain multiple items.

Requested Item (RITM): Represents a specific product or service ordered within the cart (e.g., "Developer Laptop" or "VPN Access"). Each RITM runs its own fulfillment logic and workflow.

Catalog Task (SCTASK): The actual work unit assigned to a specific group or person to fulfill the item (e.g., "Configure Laptop Hardware" or "Grant AD Group Access").

## 3. Database Table Schema Reference

ServiceNow stores catalog configurations and transactional data in specific system tables.

### 4. End-to-End Fulfillment Lifecycle Flow

+-------------------+       +--------------------+       +---------------------+       +-------------------+

| 1. Form Submission| ----> | 2. REQ Generation  | ----> | 3. RITM Execution   | ----> | 4. SCTASK Work    |

| User submits item |       | Cart creates REQ   |       | Trigger Flow/Workflow|       | Fulfillers complete|

+-------------------+       +--------------------+       +---------------------+       +-------------------+

│

▼

+-------------------+

| 5. Item Closure   |

| RITM & REQ Close  |

+-------------------+

### Detailed Lifecycle Steps

Submission: The user selects an item, fills in variables, and submits the form via Service Portal or Now Mobile.

Order Generation: ServiceNow generates a sc_request record (REQ). High-level approvals (like manager approval for total spend) execute at this tier if configured.

Item Initialization: A sc_req_item (RITM) record is generated under the REQ. The assigned Flow Designer flow or workflow starts automatically.

Task Assignment: The flow creates one or more sc_task (SCTASK) records assigned to specific teams (e.g., IT Helpdesk, Network Admin).

Closure: Once all SCTASK records are marked Closed Complete, the flow updates the RITM state to Closed Complete. Once all RITMs under a REQ are complete, the REQ is automatically closed.

## 1. Overview & Objectives

Creating a catalog item in ServiceNow involves configuring core administrative fields, portal presentation settings, access controls, and attaching a fulfillment process.

Administrators and developers can create items using either the native Service Catalog Module or the Catalog Builder interface.

### 2. Step-by-Step Procedure to Create a Catalog Item

1.Navigate to Catalog Items Module:System Administrator or Catalog Admin role required.

In the Application Navigator, go to Service Catalog > Catalog Definitions > Maintain Items. Click the New button at the top of the list view.

### 2.Configure Core Information:Populate essential identification fields.

Fill in the Name, Catalog, and Category fields to define where the item will be located and what users will see.

### 3.Attach Process Engine:Define execution engine.

In the Process Engine tab, select the appropriate Flow (Flow Designer) or Workflow that will execute upon submission.

### 4.Configure Portal Presentation:Optimize for Service Portal view.

Upload an icon and desktop picture, set search keywords, and write a clear Short Description and Description.

### 5.Save and Test:Verify in Service Portal.

Click Submit or Right-Click Header > Save. Click Try It or open the item in Service Portal to test display rendering.

The Portal Settings tab on the catalog item record controls how the item behaves and renders inside the Service Portal (/sp).

### Key Portal Configuration Flags

Hide Add to Cart: Hides the "Add to Cart" button, forcing immediate single-item ordering.

Hide Quantity: Hides the quantity dropdown selector (ideal for access requests where requesting "2 accesses" makes no sense).

Mandatory Attachment: Forces the user to attach at least one file before submitting the form.

Hide Attachment: Prevents users from attaching files to the form submission entirely.

Use Cart Layout: Inherits global shopping cart button layouts defined in catalog properties.

## 1. Overview & Objectives

A Variable Set is a modular collection of variables that can be created once and shared across multiple Catalog Items. This eliminates duplicate effort and enforces consistency across the Service Catalog.

ServiceNow offers two primary types of Variable Sets:

Single-Row Variable Sets (Standard): Organizes fields into reusable sections or containers (e.g., standard "Requester Information" block).

Multi-Row Variable Sets (MRVS): Displays as an interactive grid/table allowing users to add, edit, and remove multiple rows of structured dynamic data during a single request (e.g., ordering software licenses for 10 employees).

### 2. Comparison: Single-Row vs. Multi-Row Variable Sets

### 3. Creating & Configuring a Multi-Row Variable Set (MRVS)

### 1.Navigate to Variable Sets Module:Application Navigator navigation.

### Go to Service Catalog > Catalog Variables > Variable Sets and click New.

### 2.Choose Set Type:Select set classification.

### Select Multi-Row Variable Set from the selection dialog.

### 3.Define MRVS Core Properties:Set operational limits and names.

### Title: Visual header displayed on the form (e.g., Access Entitlements).

### Internal Name: Database name used in scripts (e.g., access_entitlements_mrvs).

### Max Rows: Optional numeric limit restricting maximum entries (e.g., 10).

### 4.Add Variables to the MRVS:Add individual inputs to the set.

Open the newly saved MRVS record. In the Variables related list, click New to define columns (e.g., System Name, Role, Access Expiration).

### 5.Associate Set to Items:Link to Catalog Items.

In the Included In related list, link the MRVS to all target Catalog Items where this grid should appear.

## 1. Overview & Objectives

Catalog Client Scripts run in the user's browser to control form behavior dynamically. They allow developers to validate user inputs, populate field values automatically, hide or show fields based on complex logic, and alter form behavior in real time before submission.

Unlike standard Client Scripts that execute on core table forms (like incident or change_request), Catalog Client Scripts are configured explicitly for catalog items, target specific catalog variables, and utilize catalog-aware g_form APIs.

## 4. Understanding Data Lookup Rules

Catalog Data Lookup Rules allow automatic population of catalog variables based on combinations of input variables. They map directly to predefined decision matrices stored in lookup tables without using server-side scripts.

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

|                            Catalog Data Lookup Engine                             |

+-----------------------------------++----------------------------------------------+

| Input Variable Values             || Output Variable Values                       |

+-----------------------------------++----------------------------------------------+

| Environment = Production          || Approval Needed = Executive Approver          |

| Urgency     = High                || Priority        = Critical (1)               |

+-----------------------------------++----------------------------------------------+

### Key Data Lookup Setup Steps

Define a Matcher Table: Create a custom table inheriting from dl_matcher or use standard lookup tables.

Set Input Variables: Map catalog variables that serve as criteria (e.g., Software Category, Region).

Set Output Variables: Map catalog variables that receive automated values (e.g., Fulfillment Group, Cost Center).

## 1. Overview & Objectives

User Criteria defines access controls for the Service Catalog by restricting or granting access to Catalog Items and Categories. It determines who can view, request, or search for specific catalog items based on user attributes such as roles, groups, departments, locations, or custom scripts.

Instead of hardcoding access controls inside forms or client scripts, User Criteria provides a centralized, reusable entitlement engine managed via the sys_user_criteria table.

### 2. Catalog Entitlement Model: Available vs. Not Available

ServiceNow uses two opposing lists to evaluate catalog visibility:

[ User Attempts to Access Item ]

│

▼

+-------------------------------------+

| Is user in "Not Available For"?     |

+-------------------------------------+

│               │

YES   │               │ NO

▼               ▼

[ DENY ACCESS ]   +-------------------------------------+

| Is user in "Available For"?         |

+-------------------------------------+

│               │

YES   │               │ NO

▼               ▼

[ GRANT ACCESS ]   [ DENY ACCESS ]

### Evaluation Rules Matrix

## 3. Deployment Lifecycle via Update Sets

All catalog items, variables, scripts, and UI policies developed in a non-production instance must be captured cleanly within an Update Set for migration.

### 1.Create and Select Update Set:Capture developer changes.

Navigate to System Update Sets > Current Update Set. Click New to create a fresh update set (e.g., STOR-10423_New_Developer_Laptop_Catalog_Item), set it to In Progress, and make it your current working update set.

### 2.Build and Configure Catalog Item:Ensure all components log to update set.

Create the catalog item, variables, variable sets, catalog client scripts, UI policies, and Flow Designer flows. (Note: Ensure Flow Designer flows are explicitly published so they register in the update set).

### 3.Complete the Update Set:Mark set ready for migration.

Navigate back to System Update Sets > Local Update Sets, open your update set record, change the State to Complete, and click Save.

4.Preview and Commit in Test/Production:Retrieve and preview in Target Instance.

In the target environment, navigate to Retrieved Update Sets, fetch the update set from the source instance, run Preview Update Set, resolve any configuration conflicts, and click Commit Update Set.

### Critical Tables Captured in Update Sets

## 4. Testing & Validation Checklist

Before releasing a catalog item to production, perform validation using ServiceNow’s Impersonate User feature to test security and rendering across different personas.

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

|                              Testing Matrix Persona                               |

+----------------------+--------------------+--------------------+------------------+

| Persona              | Purpose            | View Check         | Action Check     |

+----------------------+--------------------+--------------------+------------------+

| End User (US)        | Entitlement check  | Visible in Portal  | Can Submit       |

| End User (EU)        | Negative test      | Hidden by Criteria | Denied Access    |

| Approver / Manager   | Workflow test      | Approval Received  | Approve/Reject   |

| Fulfillment Tech     | Task work check    | Task Created       | Complete Task    |

+----------------------+--------------------+--------------------+------------------+

### Pre-Release Validation Steps

User Criteria Verification: Impersonate a user who should have access, and one who should not, to ensure correct visibility in the Service Portal.

Variable Validation: Test mandatory fields, regex patterns (e.g., email or phone formatting), and client-side onChange actions.

Workflow Execution: Submit a test request and track the resulting REQ, RITM, and SCTASK records to ensure approvals route to the right managers and tasks land in the correct assignment groups.

Service Portal Rendering: Verify that mobile, tablet, and desktop viewports render containers, column splits, and variable sets correctly without overlapping fields.

## 5. Catalog Item Deactivation & Archiving Best Practices

When an item is no longer offered or supported, never delete the catalog item record. Deleting an sc_cat_item record breaks historical reporting and corrupts legacy sc_req_item and sc_task records linked to that item ID.

### Recommended Retirement Steps

Uncheck Active: Set Active = false on the sc_cat_item record. This instantly hides the item from Service Portal searches and list views while preserving historical transaction data.

Remove Category: Clear the Category field so it no longer appears in category taxonomies.

Update Short Description: Prefix the title or short description with [RETIRED] for administrative clarity (e.g., [RETIRED] Request iPhone 11).

## 5. Catalog Item Deactivation & Archiving Best Practices

When an item is no longer offered or supported, never delete the catalog item record. Deleting an sc_cat_item record breaks historical reporting and corrupts legacy sc_req_item and sc_task records linked to that item ID.

### Recommended Retirement Steps

Uncheck Active: Set Active = false on the sc_cat_item record. This instantly hides the item from Service Portal searches and list views while preserving historical transaction data.

Remove Category: Clear the Category field so it no longer appears in category taxonomies.

Update Short Description: Prefix the title or short description with [RETIRED] for administrative clarity (e.g., [RETIRED] Request iPhone 11).

- **Examples**: Diatrace, SolarWinds, Nagios.

  - **Metrics Monitored**: CPU load, disk usage, memory usage, etc.
  - **Alert Rules**: Events are evaluated against alert rules; valid events generate alerts, incidents, problems, or changes automatically.
  - **Auto‑Closure**: Alerts are automatically closed when the underlying issue is resolved (e.g., free disk space rises above threshold).
  - **Integration Hub**: Triggers remediation actions such as running network scripts, restarting services, or provisioning virtual networks.
  - **Event Table**: `em_events` table stores events; rotated daily, older than five days are cleared.
  - **Alert Lifecycle**: Alerts can be acknowledged, decayed, traced, triggered, or remediated via the integration hub.
  - **Impact Visibility**: Alerts reflect impact on both infrastructure devices and application services.
  - **Key Features**:
    - Consolidates events from multiple sources.
    - Filters noise to generate qualified events.
    - Automates alert creation and resolution based on defined rules.

## [12:10] System Architecture Overview
- Customer network connects to **SCOM/SolarWinds**, SNMP traps, and other external monitors.  
- Events are received by the **Mix Server**, processed, and forwarded to **ServiceNow** via the **Rusty API**.  
- The **Rusty API** only receives these signals and creates event‑management entries.  
- Event processing occurs through **event truths**; a backend scheduled job runs every **5 seconds** to apply event rules.  
- After rule application, an **alert** is created or discarded accordingly.  
- The API performs **post operations** to the event table and schedules periodic jobs to enforce event rules.

## [16:00] Event and Alert Management

- **Incident Creation & Auto‑Close**
  - Alerts that resolve within **5 minutes** are automatically closed.
  - No manual intervention required from the service desk; the system handles incident lifecycle.
  - Incident creation is triggered when an alert is generated; the incident is auto‑closed when the underlying event resolves.

- **Event Ingestion Flow**
  - Events are first inserted into the **Event Table**.
  - A **scheduled job** processes events every **5 seconds**.
  - The job resolves the event to a **CIID** and registers it in the **EM Register Node Table**.

- **Alert Generation**
  - Based on event severity, an alert is inserted into the **Alert Table** as **Warning** or **Critical**.
  - Severity is calculated automatically and reflected in the operator workspace.

- **Operator Workspace Visualization**
  - Alerts, metrics, incidents, and road‑car analysis are displayed in the **Operator Workspace**.
  - The workspace provides a global view of service health and incident status.

## [24:00] Operator Workspace Overview

- **Operator Workspace** (alternative to Agent Workspace) provides a consolidated view of application service states.  
- **Event Management Operator Workspace**  
  - Displays service states in a **single view**.  
  - Statuses are color‑coded; services can be grouped, summarized, and drilled down.  
  - Clicking an item reveals:  
    - Primary alert source  
    - Service details  
    - Associated service map  
    - Business functionality  
    - Cost, location, and service group information  
- **Alert Intelligence Workspace**  
  - Selecting “All Alerts” lists alert types and offers options to run remediation tasks or engage infrastructure personnel.  
- **Dependency View Map vs. Application Service Map**  
  - **Dependency View Map**: shows server‑to‑service relationships and normal CIs; may not display alert colors or incident indicators.  
  - **Application Service Map**: presents service topology from service mapping; alerts are shown per application with color indicators (red, blue, etc.).  
  - Application map includes upstream/downstream CIs and connects alerts to the system.  
- **Boundary Alerts & Impact Severity**  
  - Alerts are color‑coded (green, red, orange) to indicate severity.  
  - In the dependency view, alerts may not appear even if incidents exist; the application service map will display the color status.  
- **Mapped Application Severity**  
  - The mapped application view shows severity levels; further inspection can be performed to verify alert details.  
- **Additional Observations from Transcript**  
  - In the **Dependency View Map**, alerts are often invisible; only CIs are displayed.  
  - The **Application Service Map** clearly shows color‑coded alerts (green, red, orange) based on alerts created against the CA.  
  - The **Mapped Application** view displays severity and allows deeper inspection when an item is clicked.  
  - In **Agent Workspace**, the **Operator Workspace** is referred to as the **Service Group** view.  
  - Clicking on the **Service Map** within the Service Group reveals service details and associated alerts.

## [34:18] Common Service Data Model (CSDM)

- **Framework Overview**
  - Standardizes CMDB data and relationships.
  - Enhances CMDB health and provides a structured approach to service management.

- **Key Components & Relationships**
  - **Business Capabilities** → linked to **Business Applications**  
  - **Business Applications** → linked to **Services**  
  - **Services** → contain **Service Offerings** and **Service Catalog**  
  - **Service Catalog** → derived from **Asset Management** (hardware or software assets)  
  - **Application** → sourced from **APM Management** (investment portfolio, technical services)  
  - **ITOM** – includes four modules that support operations.  
  - **Extended Scope**  
    - **ITAM** (IT Asset Management) is part of the service offering.  
    - **TPM** (Telecom Portfolio Management) falls under the broader CSDM umbrella.  
    - **Telecom Service Management (TSM)** and **Telecom Portfolio Management (TPM)** are integrated into the model, focusing on telecom services and related CIS processes.

- **Additional Details from Recent Transcript (36:01–40:34)**
  - **Investment Portfolio & Technical Services**  
    - Highlighted as core components within the CSDM framework.
  - **ITOM Modules**  
    - Four distinct modules identified; crucial for operational support.
  - **TPM Integration**  
    - Explicitly stated that TPM is encompassed within the CSDM model.
  - **Telecom Services Overview**  
    - **TSM & TPM**: manage satellite, 5G, 4G, SIM services, RATs, units, towers, and signal paths.  
    - These elements fall under the telecom service management scope.
  - **CMDB Configuration Best Practices**  
    - Emphasis on developing and configuring the CMDB according to CSDM principles.  
    - Implementation typically requires **over a year** for proper setup.
  - **Recommended Tables for Review**  
    - Business Capabilities  
    - Business Application  
    - Application Service  
    - Service Operating  
    - All sourced from **APM (Application Portfolio Management)**.
  - **Illustrative Example**  
    - **Application**: Ruby  
    - **Service**: Ruby on Rails  
    - Associated **Business Capabilities** and **Business Applications** are mapped.  
    - Analysis includes user counts, incident creation, alerts, and issue tracking.
  - **Business Capability Measurements**  
    - Metrics are captured within the system to assess performance and health.

## [48:03] Stable Rotation Groups and Event Lifecycle

- **Stable Rotation Groups**  
  - Define how long events remain in the system before automatic cleanup.  
  - Configurable retention periods: 5 days, 7 days, 10 days, etc.  
  - After the set period, events are **removed** from the system.

- **ECCQ (Event Control Queue)**  
  - Also governed by stable rotation.  
  - Default buffer time is **7 days** “out of the box.”  
  - The buffer ensures events are retained long enough for processing but not indefinitely.

- **Buffer Time Concept**  
  - Approximate buffer time for all events under rotations is **7 days**.  
  - This buffer applies to ECCQ and other event types.

- **Event Report Fields**  
  - When an event report is created, the system populates a set of predefined fields.  
  - Example field values are shown in the transcript; each field has a clear **description**.  
  - Users can review these fields and their meanings to understand the data captured in each report.
